transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-05-14
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 75m
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Samira Patel (Redwood AE), Diego Ramos (Redwood SE), Maya Chen (Redwood SRE); Alex Morgan (CTO - PolarPeak), Priya Singh (ML Infra), Jordan Lee (SRE)

Summary (auto): deep dive on GPU runtime profiling — kernel selection, TRT-LLM vs v L L M, cuda graphs, KV caching, batching, quantization, VPC questions.

Transcript:
[00:00] Samira: hey everyone, thanks for joining, we'll do quick intros, Diego's gonna lead the performance profiling bits and Maya will cover some of our CUDA graph notes. Alex, Priya, Jordan — want to give a 1-minute context?
[00:24] Alex: yeah thanks, so PolarPeak runs an 8x A100 on-prem cluster, using a mix of 7B and 13B models for embeddings and chat ops. Main ask is lower p50 latency for streaming responses and predictable throughput for high-concurrency inference. We're evaluating TRT-LLM and vLLM as runtimes, and curious how CUDA graphs help when we have repeated prompt shapes.
[00:46] Priya: we also have strict VPC networking and KMS for keys, so any on-prem deploy needs to play nice with our HSM and audit log requirements.
[01:05] Diego: great, that's helpful. quick agenda — kernel selection, then TRT-LLM vs vLLM numbers, followed by CUDA graphs, KV cache and batching, and finally quantization tradeoffs. we'll leave 10-15 for Qs.
[01:22] Jordan: sounds good.

[03:10] Diego: starting with kernel selection heuristics — our runtime looks at model arch, tensor shapes, sequence length distribution to pick kernels. For example, for attention we pick different kernels for small seqs (<128) vs long seqs (>1024). in TRT-LLM the plugin picks fused attention kernels which reduce kernel launches, plus TensorRT's workspace planning can give big wins. sometimes docs call it "TenserRT" which is, uh, a transcribe issue.
[03:48] Alex: is that automated or do you tune per-model?
[03:55] Diego: mostly automated — we profile during model onboarding and store preferred kernel set per model+seq-profile. but users can override; for special sequences we fall back to a safer kernel. we capture CUDA graphs on hot paths to replay the exact kernel sequence which avoids launch jitter.
[04:20] Priya: we've seen in-house that vLLM has good batching but sometimes worse tail latency under high concurrency. do you see that?
[04:35] Diego: yes, v L L M's scheduler is great for maximizing throughput, but it sometimes queues to increase GPU utilization which increases tail latency; TRT-LLM's fused kernels and optimized memory planning give lower per-token latency in many cases, especially single-request streaming. but it's model and shape dependent.

[06:00] Maya: jumping in on CUDA graphs — they shine when the sequence of kernel launches is repeatable. if your workload has stable prompt shapes or you warm the model with representative requests, replaying CUDA graphs avoids driver/kernel launch overhead. we usually see 10-30% latency improvement on stable workloads. caveat: graphs need re-capture if dynamic shapes change (like variable batch dims).
[06:27] Alex: and for KV cache heavy ops — does capturing graphs interfere?
[06:32] Diego: good q. capturing graphs with KV cache is trickier; when KV cache growth changes memory addresses or shapes, the graph can't be reused. we work around this by capturing per-step graphs for the decoder loop and using parameterized allocations so the shape remains consistent; sometimes we do "KV-slab" allocation to keep addresses stable. transcription might say K V cache as K V, just FYI.

[08:15] Priya: what about memory and workspace planning under TensorRT — any gotchas with 8xA100 NVLinks?
[08:25] Maya: with NVLink and multi-GPU you need to be careful about where you pin KV cache. TRT-LLM tends to put weights and activations per-device and relies on NCCL for cross-device comms; for extremely long contexts we recommend admin-level planning: reserve extra workspace for cuBLAS/Trt and avoid oversubscription. we can provide a YAML with recommended pinnings.

[10:10] Diego: we ran a small comparison on a 8xA100 host (this is Diego's local lab numbers, not customer yet): model 13B, seq 512, batch1 streaming, vLLM p50 ~14.2ms/token, p95 ~38ms; TRT-LLM p50 ~9.8ms/token, p95 ~21ms when using fused kernels + CUDA graphs. when enabling high-efficiency batching vLLM throughput was higher for 8k tokens but tail latency suffered. we'll share the spreadsheet.
[11:05] Alex: those p95 improvements are compelling. can we reproduce on our infra?
[11:13] Diego: yes — Diego: we'll plan to run end-to-end on your 8xA100 with your network config. Samira: I'll share the bench harness.

[13:00] Priya: about quantization — we saw accuracy drop with int8 on some instruction-tuned models. how do you recommend quant profiles?
[13:10] Maya: recommended pattern: start with fp16 runtimes, then try symmetric 4-bit or GPTQ-style 4-bit with per-channel scales. TRT-LLM supports 4-bit-aware kernels; quality can be maintained with outlier handling. for int8, only use it after acceptance tests; we do evals on held-out prompts. we can run a quality regression on your prompt set.
[13:45] Alex: is model compilation time an issue with TensorRT?
[13:50] Diego: initial compilation/engine building for TRT can take minutes to hours depending on HL ops and tactic selection. we use a cache layer so engineers build once during onboarding and then reuse optimized engines. vLLM has much faster startup but less aggressive per-op fusion. it's a tradeoff: longer onboarding compile for lower steady-state latency.

[16:30] Jordan: networking and VPC concerns — we need audit logs and our HSM. how does Redwood private handle key management?
[16:40] Samira: Redwood Private supports customer KMS/HSM integration, audit logs, and can be deployed in VPC with private control plane. we'll share SOC2/ISO artifacts and an architecture doc.

[18:05] Priya: any special notes on batching strategy for mixed workloads (embeddings + chat)?
[18:15] Diego: yes mixing workloads is tough — embeddings are small and high qps, chat is long-seq. we recommend routing by policy: small requests go to a small-model pool optimized for embeddings and batched aggressively; chat goes to dedicated pools with KV cache enabled and lower batch targets. Redwood can auto-route by model and latency SLO.

[21:00] Alex: about kernel fallbacks — we've had crashes in custom kernels in other runtimes. how do you protect production?
[21:10] Maya: we maintain a fallback policy: if an optimized kernel fails or if CUDA graph replays diverge, we revert to the safe baseline kernel (reference attention) and surface an alert. also hardware errors get mapped to node-level drains and retries.

[25:00] Diego: quick note on metrics to capture during the bench — p50/p95 token latency, tokens/sec (throughput), GPU utilization, SM efficiency, memory headroom, cuda graph replay success rate, kernel launch counts. we'll provide the Prometheus + trace queries.

[29:40] Priya: any tips for KV cache sizing for very long contexts? we sometimes see OOM at 32k sequences.
[29:50] Diego: for 32k context, you need to shard KV across devices and use quantized KV to reduce memory; also use prefix caching only for hot prompts. another strategy is progressive rollout: keep recent tokens in fast KV and older ones on slower storage and fetch on demand. TRT-LLM supports KV eviction strategies when combined with our routing layer.

[33:10] Alex: what's typical speedup from 4-bit quant + TRT kernels vs fp16?
[33:20] Maya: often 1.5x-2x throughput, but accuracy delta varies. for some LLMs you can hit ~1.8x throughput with well-tuned 4-bit, sometimes higher when memory bandwidth is the bottleneck. we always recommend regression evals.

[40:00] Diego: demo time — I want to show a short trace where CUDA graphs reduce launch jitter. (screen share) here you can see kernel timeline before and after capture — before it's scattershot, after it's compact and repeatable. note the fused attention kernel reduces memcpy and kernel spans.
[43:30] Alex: nice, can you share the trace file?
[43:35] Diego: yes will upload to the shared folder - link: https://redwood.ai/bench/trace-pp-20260514 (placeholder)

[46:00] Priya: any pitfalls with NCCL/allreduce in multi-node setups when using TRT-LLM?
[46:10] Maya: yes — NCCL tuning matters. ensure matching NCCL versions and allow fingerprinting of network topology. for multi-node, we recommend bandwidth testing and sometimes pinning comm threads away from CUDA graph replay threads to avoid contention.

[50:00] Jordan: security Q: are compiled TensorRT engines deterministic and auditable? our legal team asks for reproducible builds.
[50:10] Samira: engines are deterministic given the same tactics and GPU driver stack, but tactic selection might vary with driver/hardware. we store the engine binary and capture the build metadata (driver, cudnn, trt version, tactic seeds) so you can reproduce. we'll include those artifacts in the onboarding package.

[58:00] Priya: customer-specific ask: can Redwood run a pilot with mix of streaming and batch models for 30 days?
[58:10] Samira: yes — typical pilot is 30-60 days, we can provision a dedicated pool in your VPC or run on your infra if you prefer. we'll prepare a scope doc.

[65:00] Diego: wrapping up — next steps recap: Diego will run the bench on your cluster, Samira will share the spreadsheet and docs, Maya will send CUDA graph + kernel notes, Priya will provide deployment YAML and compliance q's.
[65:30] Alex: thanks everyone, this was super useful.
[66:00] Samira: thanks all, we'll follow up with calendar for the results review in the week of May 25.

End of transcript.
